{{short description|Connects the homology of the symmetric groups with mapping spaces of spheres}}
In [[homotopy theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], the '''Barratt–Priddy theorem''' (also referred to as '''Barratt–Priddy–Quillen theorem''') expresses a connection between the homology of the [[symmetric group]]s and mapping spaces of spheres. The theorem (named after Michael Barratt, Stewart Priddy, and [[Daniel Quillen]]) is also often stated as a relation between the [[sphere spectrum]] and the [[classifying space]]s of the symmetric groups via Quillen's [[plus construction]].

==Statement of the theorem==

The mapping space <math>\operatorname{Map}_0(S^n,S^n)</math> is the [[topological space]] of all continuous maps <math>f\colon S^n \to S^n</math> from the {{mvar|n}}-dimensional sphere <math>S^n</math> to itself, under the topology of [[uniform convergence]] (a special case of the [[compact-open topology]]). These maps are required to fix a basepoint <math>x\in S^n</math>, satisfying <math>f(x)=x</math>, and to have [[degree of a continuous mapping|degree]] 0; this guarantees that the mapping space is [[connected space|connected]]. The Barratt–Priddy theorem expresses a relation between the homology of these mapping spaces and the homology of the [[symmetric group]]s <math>\Sigma_n</math>.

It follows from the [[Freudenthal suspension theorem]] and the [[Hurewicz theorem]] that the {{mvar|k}}th [[homology theory|homology]] <math>H_k(\operatorname{Map}_0(S^n,S^n))</math> of this mapping space is ''independent'' of the dimension {{mvar|n}}, as long as <math>n>k</math>. Similarly, {{harvs|txt|first=Minoru|last=Nakaoka|year=1960}} proved that the {{mvar|k}}th [[group homology]] <math>H_k(\Sigma_n)</math> of the symmetric group <math>\Sigma_n</math> on {{mvar|n}} elements is independent of {{mvar|n}}, as long as <math>n \ge 2k</math>. This is an instance of [[homological stability]].

The Barratt–Priddy theorem states that these "stable homology groups" are the same: for <math>n \ge 2k</math>, there is a natural isomorphism

:<math>H_k(\Sigma_n)\cong H_k(\text{Map}_0(S^n,S^n)).</math>

This isomorphism holds with integral coefficients (in fact with any coefficients, as is made clear in the reformulation below).

==Example: first homology==

This isomorphism can be seen explicitly for the first homology <math>H_1</math>. The [[Group cohomology#H1|first homology of a group]] is the largest [[abelian group|commutative]] quotient of that group. For the permutation groups <math>\Sigma_n</math>, the only commutative quotient is given by the [[sign of a permutation]], taking values in {{math|{−1, 1}}}. This shows that <math>H_1(\Sigma_n) \cong \Z/2\Z</math>, the [[cyclic group]] of order 2, for all <math>n\ge 2</math>. (For <math>n= 1</math>, <math>\Sigma_1</math> is the [[trivial group]], so <math>H_1(\Sigma_1) = 0</math>.)

It follows from the theory of [[covering space]]s that the mapping space <math>\operatorname{Map}_0(S^1,S^1)</math> of the circle <math>S^1</math> is [[contractible space|contractible]], so
<math>H_1(\operatorname{Map}_0(S^1,S^1))=0</math>. For the 2-sphere <math>S^2</math>, the first [[homotopy group]] and first homology group of the mapping space are [[Homotopy groups of spheres#.CF.803.28S2.29 .3D Z|both infinite cyclic]]:
:<math>\pi_1(\operatorname{Map}_0(S^2,S^2))=H_1(\operatorname{Map}_0(S^2,S^2))\cong \Z</math>. 

A generator for this group can be built from the [[Hopf fibration]] <math>S^3 \to S^2</math>. Finally, once <math>n\ge 3</math>, both are [[Homotopy groups of spheres#Table of homotopy groups|cyclic of order 2]]:
:<math>\pi_1(\operatorname{Map}_0(S^n,S^n))=H_1(\operatorname{Map}_0(S^n,S^n))\cong \Z/2\Z</math>. 

==Reformulation of the theorem==
The infinite symmetric group <math>\Sigma_{\infty}</math> is the union of the finite [[symmetric group]]s <math>\Sigma_{n}</math>, and Nakaoka's theorem implies that the group homology of <math>\Sigma_{\infty}</math> is the stable homology of <math>\Sigma_{n}</math>: for <math>n\ge 2k</math>, 
:<math>H_k(\Sigma_{\infty}) \cong H_k(\Sigma_{n})</math>.
The [[classifying space]] of this group is denoted <math>B \Sigma_{\infty}</math>, and its homology of this space is the group homology of <math>\Sigma_{\infty}</math>: 
:<math>H_k(B \Sigma_{\infty})\cong H_k(\Sigma_{\infty})</math>.

We similarly denote by <math>\operatorname{Map}_0(S^{\infty},S^{\infty})</math> the union of the mapping spaces <math>\operatorname{Map}_0(S^{n},S^{n})</math> under the inclusions induced by [[suspension (topology)|suspension]]. The homology of <math>\operatorname{Map}_0(S^{\infty},S^{\infty})</math> is the stable homology of the previous mapping spaces: for <math>n>k</math>, 
:<math>H_k(\operatorname{Map}_0(S^{\infty},S^{\infty})) \cong H_k(\operatorname{Map}_0(S^{n},S^{n})).</math>

There is a natural map <math>\varphi\colon B\Sigma_{\infty} \to \operatorname{Map}_0(S^{\infty},S^{\infty})</math>; one way to construct this map is via the model of <math>B\Sigma_{\infty}</math> as the space of finite subsets of <math>\R^{\infty}</math> endowed with an appropriate topology. An equivalent formulation of the Barratt–Priddy theorem is that <math>\varphi</math> is a ''homology equivalence'' (or ''acyclic map''), meaning that <math>\varphi</math> induces an isomorphism on all homology groups with any local coefficient system.

==Relation with Quillen's plus construction==
The Barratt–Priddy theorem implies that the space {{math|''BΣ''<sub>∞</sub><sup>+</sup>}} resulting from applying Quillen's [[plus construction]]  to {{math|''BΣ''<sub>∞</sub>}} can be identified with {{math|Map<sub>0</sub>(''S''<sup>∞</sup>,''S''<sup>∞</sup>)}}. (Since {{math|&pi;<sub>1</sub>(Map<sub>0</sub>(''S''<sup>∞</sup>,''S''<sup>∞</sup>))≅''H''<sub>1</sub>(''Σ''<sub>∞</sub>)≅'''Z'''/2'''Z'''}}, the map {{math|''φ'': ''BΣ''<sub>∞</sub>→Map<sub>0</sub>(''S''<sup>∞</sup>,''S''<sup>∞</sup>)}} satisfies the universal property of the plus construction once it is known that {{mvar|φ}} is a homology equivalence.)

The mapping spaces {{math|Map<sub>0</sub>(''S''<sup>''n''</sup>,''S''<sup>''n''</sup>)}} are more commonly denoted by {{math|''Ω''<sup>''n''</sup><sub>0</sub>''S''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, where {{math|''Ω''<sup>''n''</sup>''S''<sup>''n''</sup>}} is the {{mvar|n}}-fold [[loop space]] of the {{mvar|n}}-sphere {{mvar|S<sup>n</sup>}}, and similarly {{math|Map<sub>0</sub>(''S''<sup>∞</sup>,''S''<sup>∞</sup>)}} is denoted by {{math|''Ω''<sup>∞</sup><sub>0</sub>''S''<sup>∞</sup>}}. Therefore the Barratt–Priddy theorem can also be stated as

:<math>B\Sigma_\infty^+\simeq \Omega_0^\infty S^\infty</math> or

:<math>\textbf{Z}\times B\Sigma_\infty^+\simeq \Omega^\infty S^\infty</math>

In particular, the homotopy groups of {{math|''BΣ''<sub>∞</sub><sup>+</sup>}} are the [[homotopy groups of spheres|stable homotopy groups of spheres]]:

:<math>\pi_i(B\Sigma_\infty^+)\cong \pi_i(\Omega^\infty S^\infty)\cong \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \pi_{n+i}(S^n)=\pi_i^s(S^n)</math>

=="''K''-theory of '''F'''<sub>1</sub>"==

The Barratt–Priddy theorem is sometimes colloquially rephrased as saying that "the ''K''-groups of '''F'''<sub>1</sub> are the stable homotopy groups of spheres". This is not a meaningful mathematical statement, but a metaphor expressing an analogy with [[algebraic K-theory|algebraic ''K''-theory]].

The "[[field with one element]]" '''F'''<sub>1</sub> is not a [[mathematical object]]; it refers to a collection of analogies between algebra and combinatorics. One central analogy is the idea that {{math|''GL''<sub>''n''</sub>('''F'''<sub>1</sub>)}} should be the symmetric group {{math|''Σ''<sub>''n''</sub>}}.
The [[Algebraic K-theory#Higher K-theory|higher ''K''-groups]] {{math|''K''<sub>''i''</sub>(''R'')}} of a ring ''R'' can be defined as
:<math>K_i(R)=\pi_i(BGL_\infty(R)^+)</math>

According to this analogy, the K-groups {{math|''K''<sub>''i''</sub>('''F'''<sub>1</sub>)}} of {{math|'''F'''<sub>1</sub>}} should be defined as {{math|&pi;<sub>''i''</sub>(''BGL''<sub>∞</sub>('''F'''<sub>1</sub>)<sup>+</sup>){{=}}&pi;<sub>''i''</sub>(''BΣ''<sub>∞</sub><sup>+</sup>)}}, which by the Barratt–Priddy theorem is:
:<math>K_i(\mathbf{F}_1)=\pi_i(BGL_\infty(\mathbf{F}_1)^+)=\pi_i(B\Sigma_\infty^+)=\pi_i^s.</math>
